name: The Age of Coming
summary: The ruins of the first age had owners: a lighthouse lit for a brother who never woke, a mill brought by a woman who hated it, a face nobody can ask about — and then the first wall went soft.
body: Walk east from [[lore/the_waking|the meadow]] for an afternoon and you will pass under a broken aqueduct, through a ring of standing stones, past a windmill with its sails still rigged, and along a line of poles strung with wire that runs from nowhere to nowhere. None of these things belong in the same world. All of them are here.

The dead arrive from everywhere and every when, and here remembering is not a private event: a thing held firmly enough, long enough, in enough minds, simply is. Somebody woke knowing exactly what an aqueduct was — knew it the way you know the stairs of your childhood house — and so there is an aqueduct. The oldest call that first stretch of the world's history the Age of Coming. No maintenance, no scarcity, nobody yet suspecting that anything needed keeping; the country grew larger, stranger and more beautiful, and nearly everything good to look at dates from it. But the ruins are not the lesson. The lesson is the people they belonged to. Meet three of them.

The lighthouse stands in the shallows of a sea no ship has ever crossed, and a man named Nils built it with his hands. In life his brother drowned within sight of a real one — lamp lit, keeper awake, the whole machinery of warning working exactly as intended, and his brother slipping under quietly a little way outside the light. Nils died years later, far from any coast, and woke on the meadow still listening for water. On a shore with nothing to warn he built a lighthouse anyway, and then he changed what a lighthouse is for: he lit it every evening, so that if his brother ever woke in this country — on the meadow, in the far hills, anywhere — there would be a light on the water that meant: come here. I kept it burning. His brother never woke. Nils lit the lamp anyway, every evening, for longer than most countries last, because he would not agree that it was for nobody. The lamp is cold now. The tower stands.

The windmill nobody turns was brought by a woman who hated it. She had been put to it as a girl — wind, grain, the same circle of sky — and she walked out of its shadow the day she was grown and never once looked back. She lived, she grew old somewhere with pavement under her feet, she died, she woke on the meadow. Within a season the sails stood up over the birches, because the Age of Coming never asked what you loved. It asked what you knew all the way to the bone, and what she knew, under everything she built on top of it, was the mill. She spent a long age here in its shadow, furious. You do not choose what comes with you. You are not asked.

And out on the ice there is a statue with a face nobody recognises. It was carried here on somebody's back, the whole way, over years; people still tell of the carrier on the roads, bent double, refusing carts, refusing company, setting the burden down at dusk and sitting opposite it in silence until dark. Nobody asked. Asking felt like putting a finger in a wound. Now the carrier is long gone from every road, there is no one left to ask, and the statue stands in the ice being the most important face in somebody's world — name unknown, story unknown, kept upright, the old ones say, by the wondering itself, because ten thousand travellers asking whose face is that, at ten thousand fires, is also a kind of remembering. Whoever it was is held in the world by strangers. That is either the loneliest thing in this chapter or the kindest, and nobody has settled it.

The age ended without ceremony. A man had set a triumphal arch in a field, for a victory won in a country that is not here, and for a long lifetime he told that victory to anyone who slowed down — until one year he stopped, because everyone had heard it. The carved faces on the arch went smooth first, like wax near a flame. Then a wall somewhere was not as tall as it had been, and then it was a heap, and then a green place where a heap used to be. Whole streets began to be less. Nobody understood. They blamed the winters, they blamed the ground, and there was a whole confident generation certain it had something to do with the sea.
It had nothing to do with the sea. The answer was paid for by one silent woman, and what it cost her is [[lore/the_age_of_fires|the Age of Fires]].
